questions.subject: Reading
questions.learningObjective: Infer purpose and identify actions or conditions in everyday communications.
questions.passage:
To: Student media team
Subject: Friday equipment collection

The room will open an hour later on Friday while the shelves are being moved. Anyone who booked a recorder for the first hour can collect it from the theatre office instead. Please bring your booking confirmation. The theatre office has no spare equipment, so requests for additional items must wait until the equipment room opens. Return all borrowed items to the equipment room as usual.
questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the message?
questions.answer: To explain how collections will work during a delayed opening.
questions.explanation: The message gives a temporary collection arrangement for early bookings.
options: To invite students to help move shelving.
To confirm a new permanent location for the room.
To announce new types of equipment available for loan.
To explain how collections will work during a delayed opening.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.learningObjective: Interpret details, vocabulary and relationships in a short expository passage.
questions.passageTitle: Why a queue can look shorter without moving faster
questions.passage:
Visitors who approach a busy ticket counter often estimate their wait by counting the people ahead. That strategy works fairly well when everyone makes similar requests. It becomes less reliable when transactions vary in complexity. A group buying seats together may need several minutes, even though it looks like a single customer from the back of the line.

One way to reduce uncertainty is to display the estimated remaining wait. In a fictional museum trial, the display used the recent rate of completed transactions. It reacted quickly when a second counter opened, but it underestimated delays just after a group arrived to discuss several bookings. The display could count how quickly staff had worked before the group arrived. It had no information about what the group would ask them to do.

A different solution is to direct visitors with simple requests to a separate desk. This can make estimates more reliable at that desk, because the transactions are more alike. It can also leave longer requests concentrated at the original counter. A manager evaluating the arrangement should therefore examine waiting times at both desks. Improving the apparent speed of one queue gives only a partial picture of how the service has changed.
questions.prompt: What problem does the example of the group buying seats illustrate?
questions.answer: The number of customers can conceal differences in the work required.
questions.explanation: A group can look like one customer but take much longer than a simple purchase.
options: Customers in groups usually overestimate how many seats they need.
Counting people ahead is impossible at a ticket counter.
Busy counters commonly serve groups before individual customers.
The number of customers can conceal differences in the work required.
